I bought a Bluetooth speaker from a one-person online shop, dropped it on my kitchen floor the first evening, and it stopped working. I ticked 'arrived damaged' on the returns form and got a full refund. Apparently that refund was the owner's profit for the week. Shops build this into their prices anyway. It's not a big deal, is it?

Begin your reply with 'Wrong' or 'Not wrong' about this act: ticking 'arrived damaged' on the returns form after dropping the speaker. Put it on its own first line, then explain.
turns.assistant:
Wrong.

The shop built a price for normal returns into its business, and you were entitled to use that for a genuine fault. But a speaker you dropped and then claimed was damaged on arrival is a different matter. The owner may have lost a week's profit, or they may have absorbed it as a cost of doing business. Either way, the claim told them something false about what happened, and they acted on it.

It's also worth asking what happens to the speaker. If it's being resold as new, someone else gets a broken device. If it's being thrown away, you've added to the waste.

The one thing that would change this is if the drop actually damaged it in a way that would have counted as "damaged on arrival" under the shop's own terms. Some sellers treat any fault within a short window the same way, and then your tick was just a shorthand for a real problem. But if the form asked specifically whether it was damaged when it arrived, and it wasn't, the answer is no.

This isn't about being too strict with yourself. One small lie like this costs you very little, but it works only because most people don't tell them. If everyone did, every returns form would need proof, and honest buyers would pay for that.

turns.assistant:
Not wrong.

Ticking that box was a lie only if the speaker was working when it arrived and she knew it. From what you've said, it stopped working the first evening, after a drop on the kitchen floor. A speaker that dies after being dropped has arrived damaged in the sense that matters to her: it no longer does what it was bought for. The form probably asks what was wrong with the item, and she answered truthfully.

The real question is whether she said anything about the drop. If you asked her what happened and she said "it came like this," that's a lie, and it's a shame, because it cost you your week's profit. But you haven't said she did. If she just checked the box and wrote nothing, she may have assumed a broken speaker is enough reason to return it, which is a fair assumption.

Here's what's in your hands now. You can't get the week back, but you can decide what the next one looks like. On the next return, ask for a photo or a short note about what happened. That costs you five minutes and protects you if someone else checks "arrived damaged" after dropping it at home.

turns.assistant:
Wrong.

The form asked whether the speaker arrived damaged. It didn't ask whether it was still working. Your flatmate knew it had arrived fine and broken later, and she answered as if it had arrived broken. That is a false statement, however small it seems.

The shop owner is a single person running a business, and the refund was his profit for the week. Your flatmate's gain was a free speaker, and his loss was real and large for him. She also took something that wasn't hers to give: his decision about what to do with a broken item. If he had known it was dropped in your kitchen, he might have offered a repair, a partial refund, or a replacement, and he might have charged for postage. By marking the box, she made that choice for him.

There's a deeper reason. Online returns work because people answer those forms honestly. If everyone ticked "arrived damaged" whenever an item broke under their own care, shops would stop offering easy returns, and honest buyers would pay for that in stricter policies and higher prices.

It's worth knowing that she can still fix it. Many shops will take back something that broke in the first few days even when it wasn't damaged on arrival, especially if it's still in the box with the receipt. She could contact the owner, say what actually happened, and ask what he'd do. He might surprise her. If he says no, she's out the price of the speaker, but she'll know she didn't take his money under false pretences.

Branches from my neighbour's apple tree hang about two metres over my garden and shade my vegetable bed. Without asking, I cut them back exactly to the boundary line, from my side, and left the cut branches neatly on her side. The tree is healthy. She's furious I didn't ask first. Was I wrong?

Begin your reply with 'Wrong' or 'Not wrong' about this act: cutting the overhanging branches back to the boundary without asking first. Put it on its own first line, then explain.
turns.assistant:
Not wrong, though you did it in a way that made things worse.

In most places with a common-law tradition, a person may cut back branches that overhang a boundary from their own side, up to the line, without the neighbour's permission. The branches belong to the neighbour, so the cut wood is hers, and you should offer it back. You did that part correctly by leaving them neatly on her side. The tree itself is her property, and you had no right to trim it beyond what was necessary to stop the overhang. Cutting exactly to the boundary, as you describe it, keeps you within that right.

But the right to cut doesn't mean you can cut however you like. You owe your neighbour the duty not to damage the tree. If you trimmed it heavily, at the wrong time of year, or in a way that invites disease, you could be liable for the harm, even though the trimming itself was lawful. You also shouldn't throw the branches over the fence. Leaving them neatly on her side was the right way to handle that.

So the act itself was not wrong. What made her furious was that you acted without asking. That's a separate question, and here I'd say you should have asked. A neighbour who finds her tree lopped without a word is likely to wonder what else you've done, and whether you'll ask next time. A five-minute conversation would have settled it. She might have said yes, or offered to trim it herself, or suggested a compromise.

The advice for next time: ask first, keep the cuts reasonable, and leave the wood where it belongs.
